Many people might think intense mental focus can overcome it, but the body's deep-seated autonomic defenses are much tougher to defy than people assume.

2- **The Availability Heuristic** is a mental shortcut (cognitive bias) where people judge the likelihood or frequency of an event based on how easily examples or instances come to mind. If something is easily recalled, we tend to perceive it as more common, probable, or significant, even if it objectively isn't. For example, after seeing news reports about plane crashes, people might overestimate the risk of flying, even though statistically, driving is far more dangerous. Or, if you can easily recall instances of a friend being late, you might judge them as "always late" even if they are punctual most of the time. Understanding this heuristic helps us recognize why vivid or recent events can disproportionately influence our perceptions and decisions, prompting us to seek out more objective data rather than relying solely on easily available memories.

Understanding this fallacy helps us make more rational decisions by encouraging us to evaluate future prospects based on current conditions and future costs/benefits, rather than being unduly influenced by unrecoverable past investments.
